questions.question: Everyone says threads are expensive and coroutines are lightweight, but coroutines run on threads. What resolves that?
options: Coroutines run on a special kind of lighter thread
A coroutine is an object on the heap that the scheduler never sees, and a suspended one holds no thread
Coroutines run on the GPU rather than the CPU
The runtime compiles coroutines into a single thread
questions.explanation: Cost comes from being an operating system object with a stack and a place in the scheduler's list. A coroutine is neither, which is why thousands of them can share a small pool of real threads.

questions.question: A phone has eight cores. How many threads are executing at this instant, across the whole device?
options: As many as are ready to run
Eight, one per core
One, because Android is single threaded
It depends on how many apps are in the foreground
questions.explanation: Everything beyond eight is waiting for a turn, and the appearance of more is the kernel switching quickly between them. That budget is shared by every app on the device at once.

questions.question: Why does switching between two threads in the same process cost less than switching between two processes?
options: Threads have smaller stacks than processes
The kernel does not need to save registers for a thread switch
The two threads share an address space, so the page table does not change
Thread switches happen in user space without involving the kernel
questions.explanation: Registers, the program counter and the stack pointer are saved either way. The extra cost of a process switch is swapping the page table and losing the processor's cached address translations.

questions.question: Your app crashes with "OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed". What ran out?
options: The app's heap, from allocating too many objects
Memory for one more thread's stack
The device's storage
The scheduler's list of runnable threads
questions.explanation: The message names the thing it could not get: the stack reserved for a new thread. It usually means an unbounded pool, or a library creating one thread per unit of work.

questions.question: A developer moves image processing onto Dispatchers.IO because it is "not the main thread". What is the likely result?
options: It is the correct fix, because IO is designed for heavy work
Nothing changes, because both dispatchers use the same pool
Many compute-hungry threads compete for cores, and everything including the main thread gets slower
The work runs on the GPU instead
questions.explanation: The IO pool is large because its threads are expected to sit blocked without using a core. Computation does use a core, so a large pool of it produces exactly the switching cost this lesson describes, and Dispatchers.Default is sized near the core count to prevent that.

questions.question: An app spawns one thread for each of two hundred list items. On a desktop it is fine; on a phone it stutters badly. What best explains the difference?
options: Phone CPUs cannot run threads in parallel
Android limits an app to a fixed number of threads
Fewer cores and less memory, so the same thread count means more switching and more reserved stacks
The threads are being garbage collected during the work
questions.explanation: The thread count did not change, but the number of cores to share them across did, and so did the memory available for stacks. The same code is simply asking for much more than the device has.
